lesson.title: Configuration Management: Treating Network Configs Like Code
lesson.summary: Configuration management is the practice of defining device configurations as version-controlled templates that automation applies consistently, rather than relying on someone typing the same commands correctly by hand on every device.
lesson.body:
Change control describes the process a network change should follow: request, review, scheduled window, rollback plan, verification. But that process is only as reliable as the discipline of the humans carrying it out, and it does not scale well by hand. If a change needs to be applied identically across forty switches, typing the same commands into forty separate SSH sessions is slow, tedious, and exactly the kind of repetitive manual task where a typo eventually slips through, on switch seventeen, at 2 AM, when nobody notices until later. Configuration management is the tooling that makes change control's promises actually hold at that scale.

The core idea is to store the intended configuration, not just the process for changing it, as version-controlled source of truth, usually in a git repository, and to use automation tools to apply it to real devices rather than relying on manual entry. Tools like Ansible, Puppet, or Chef, along with vendor-specific automation frameworks, read a template or intended-state definition and push the resulting configuration out to many devices consistently. Because the source of truth is just files in version control, every change to it is a commit: it has an author, a timestamp, and a diff showing exactly what changed, which is precisely the audit trail change control asks for, except produced automatically as a side effect of how the work is done, rather than depending on someone remembering to write it up separately.

This also solves a problem change control alone does not fully address: configuration drift, where devices slowly diverge from their intended configuration over time because of one-off manual fixes that never get recorded anywhere. Configuration management tools can periodically compare a device's actual running configuration against the stored source of truth and flag or correct any difference, catching drift before it becomes an outage nobody can explain.

A concrete example makes the contrast clear. Suppose a new VLAN needs to be added across forty access switches. Done manually, that means SSHing into forty devices and typing the same handful of commands into each one, with no guarantee all forty were done identically, and no record afterward of exactly what was typed where. Done with configuration management, the VLAN definition is added once, to the source-of-truth repository, and an automation playbook pushes that change out to all forty switches, logging the result of each one. If switch seventeen fails a post-change check, for instance because it is running an older software version that rejects part of the syntax, that failure is flagged immediately and explicitly, rather than silently leaving that one switch out of sync with the other thirty-nine, the kind of quiet drift that would otherwise surface weeks later as a confusing, hard-to-explain inconsistency. Every step is recorded automatically: what changed, when, by whom, and what the result was on each device, turning change control from a manual discipline someone has to remember into a property the tooling enforces.
